consensus_summary: The dominant traditional identification is the Church (or believer) as reflected light of Christ the sun, drawn from patristic allegory and texts such as Gen 1:16, Song 6:10 and Rev 12:1; other frequent but secondary uses include apocalyptic portents of judgment (darkened/blood moon), Mary, Israel/family, calendar seasons, covenant permanence and anti-idolatry polemic. No single meaning is settled.
book_summary: The moon is the faithful witness—the Son—who has no light of His own but reflects the Father’s light, shining in the world’s night as the lesser light that rules the night and marks appointed times.
consensus_core_identification: Church (or people of God) reflecting Christ’s light
book_core_identification: the Son reflecting the Father’s light
boundary_disagreement: Book replaces the consensus ecclesial/Marian/Israelite reflector with the Son Himself and relocates the light-source from Christ to the Father, thereby excluding the Church-as-moon cases that form the consensus core.
material_contradiction: Consensus primary referent (Church reflecting Christ) and book primary referent (Son reflecting Father) cannot both hold as the symbolic identity of the moon in the same sense; accepting the book requires discarding the consensus identification.
rationale: Minimum cores are Church-as-reflector versus Son-as-reflector. Both employ the same optical metaphor yet assign mutually exclusive personal referents and reverse the usual Christ/Church typology. No consensus primary or listed alternative equates the moon with Christ the Son; the book’s reassignment therefore replaces rather than narrows, broadens or overlaps the consensus core. The printed citations supply the verbal links (moon = “faithful witness,” Jesus = “faithful witness,” Son does only what He sees the Father do) that enable the reassignment but do not themselves assert the equation.
strongest_objection: The equation rests on a midrashic chaining of “faithful witness” (Ps 89:37 to Rev 1:5) and the functional parallel of reflected action (John 5:19), none of which the texts themselves apply to the moon; the overwhelming patristic and homiletic tradition keeps Christ as sun and the Church as moon, rendering the book’s inversion an unsupported novelty.
